reigns.tagline: The fisherman Jesus called the rock
reigns.cameToPower: Led the apostles after the Crucifixion
reigns.previously: Jesus is crucified. A fisherman from Galilee leads his followers.
paragraphs: His name was Simon, and he fished the Sea of Galilee with his brother Andrew until a wandering preacher called Jesus told them to follow him. In Matthew's Gospel Jesus gives Simon a new name, Peter, from the word for rock, and says: on this rock I will build my church. Peter was loud, loyal and brave, right up until the night of the arrest, when he denied knowing Jesus three times before the cock crowed.

After the Crucifixion he led the little movement in Jerusalem. The Acts of the Apostles has him preaching, healing, landing in jail and arguing with Paul over whether non-Jewish converts had to keep Jewish law. Later he seems to have reached Rome. Early Christian writers agree he died there under Nero, after the great fire of 64, when the emperor blamed the Christians and had them killed in horrible ways.

Catholics count Peter as the first bishop of Rome, and every pope since as his heir. That claim to his chair is the foundation stone of the whole papacy. By tradition his followers buried him on the Vatican Hill, close to the circus where so many of them had died.

claims.text: Peter asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die the same way as Jesus.
claims.note: The story comes from the apocryphal Acts of Peter, written in the late 2nd century, more than a hundred years after his death.

claims.text: Peter was the first bishop of Rome.
claims.note: Lists of Roman bishops starting from Peter appear in the late 2nd century, with Irenaeus. Most historians think Rome's church was led by a group of elders until well into the 2nd century.

claims.text: Peter's bones lie under the high altar of St Peter's.
claims.note: Pius XII announced in 1950 that the tomb had been found, and Paul VI said in 1968 that the bones had been identified. Archaeologists still argue over the excavations.

reigns.hook: Peter is dead, and Rome's Christians are a hunted minority. For the next 250 years their leaders will live on the wrong side of the law, and most will leave little more than a name.

reigns.title: Bishops of the Catacombs
reigns.tagline: Outlaw bishops in an empire that hunted them
reigns.previously: Peter dies a martyr in Nero's Rome.
paragraphs: After Peter come Linus, Anacletus, Clement and a long line of men who are mostly just names on a list. The lists were drawn up in the late 2nd century, and the early dates are traditional. One real voice survives. Around 96 the Roman church wrote to the Christians of Corinth, telling them to stop squabbling and respect their elders. Tradition says Clement wrote it.

Christianity was illegal, but persecution came in waves. In 250 Emperor Decius ordered everyone to sacrifice to the gods, and Bishop Fabian died for refusing. Earlier in the century Callixtus, a former slave, had run the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way that still bears his name. His bitter rival Hippolytus set up as bishop against him and is often called the first antipope. Then, from 303, came Diocletian's Great Persecution, the worst of all.

Suddenly everything flipped. In 312 Constantine beat his rival at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome and credited the Christian God. In 313 the Edict of Milan let Christians worship freely. Bishop Miltiades had lived through the hunt. He died in January 314 in a city where his faith was suddenly in fashion.

claims.text: Callixtus had been a slave who lost his master's money and was sent to the mines.
claims.note: Our only source is his enemy Hippolytus, who wrote to blacken his name.

claims.text: Constantine saw a cross in the sky with the words 'In this sign, conquer'.
claims.note: Eusebius says Constantine told him so years later. Lactantius, writing closer to the battle, mentions only a dream.

claims.text: The Roman church wrote to Corinth around 96, and the letter survives.
claims.note: The letter, known as 1 Clement, survives in full. Its link to Clement comes from 2nd-century writers such as Dionysius of Corinth.

reigns.hook: Christianity is legal and the emperor is its patron. Constantine is pouring money into Rome's churches. The bishops are about to learn what an emperor's friendship costs.

reigns.title: The Emperor's Church
reigns.tagline: Gold from the emperor, blood at the elections
reigns.previously: Constantine legalises Christianity. Bishop Miltiades dies in peace.
paragraphs: Sylvester I had the luck to be bishop when the money arrived. Constantine built a great basilica at the Lateran and handed it to the bishop of Rome, then raised the first St Peter's over the shrine on the Vatican Hill. But the emperor ran the show. When he called the Council of Nicaea in 325 to settle what Christians believed about Christ, Sylvester stayed at home and sent two priests.

Elections got ugly. In 366 the backers of Damasus fought a rival faction, and the historian Ammianus counted 137 bodies on a basilica floor in a single day. Damasus won, and proved a shrewd pope. He set his secretary Jerome to work on a new Latin Bible, the Vulgate, which the Western Church used for over a thousand years. In 380 Emperor Theodosius made Christianity the religion of the empire.

The empire was cracking. In 410 the Goth Alaric sacked Rome, the first enemy to take the city in nearly 800 years. Pope Innocent I wasn't even there. He was at Ravenna, trying to broker a deal with the emperor. Rome had lost its glory, and its bishop was turning into the most important man left in it.

claims.text: Constantine gave Sylvester and his heirs power over the whole western empire.
claims.note: This is the Donation of Constantine, a forgery of the 8th century. Lorenzo Valla proved it fake in 1440 from its anachronistic Latin.

claims.text: Sylvester cured Constantine of leprosy and baptised him.
claims.note: A later legend. Constantine was baptised on his deathbed in 337 by Eusebius of Nicomedia.

claims.text: 137 people died in one day in the fight over Damasus's election.
claims.note: The figure comes from Ammianus Marcellinus, a pagan historian writing at the time; Christian sources on the rival side blame Damasus.

reigns.hook: Rome is sacked, the West is falling apart, and worse is on the way. The next bishop will have to face the most feared man of the age, Attila the Hun.

reigns.tagline: The pope who stared down Attila
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Deacon of Rome under Sixtus III
reigns.previously: Sixtus III dies. Rome's leading deacon is away in Gaul.
paragraphs: Leo was a deacon of the Roman church, sent to Gaul to patch up a quarrel between two Roman generals, when news came that he had been elected pope. He came home and made the job bigger than anyone before him. Peter, he preached, still spoke through his heir in Rome, and bishops everywhere should listen.

The East took notice. In 449 he sent a letter on the nature of Christ, known as his Tome. At the Council of Chalcedon in 451 it helped shape the council's definition of Christ as one person with two natures, divine and human. In 452 Attila's Huns were rampaging through northern Italy. Leo rode out with two leading Romans and met him near Mantua. Attila turned back.

In 455 the Vandals under Gaiseric sailed in and took Rome. Leo met him and talked him out of burning the city and massacring its people, though the Vandals still looted it for two weeks. Leo died in November 461, the first pope buried in St Peter's. Later ages called him Leo the Great.

claims.text: Peter and Paul appeared in the sky with swords, and that is why Attila turned back.
claims.note: A later legend, painted by Raphael in the Vatican. Hunger and disease in the Hun army probably mattered more.

claims.text: At Chalcedon the bishops shouted, 'Peter has spoken through Leo!'
claims.note: The cry is recorded in the official acts of the council.

claims.text: Leo persuaded Gaiseric to spare the lives of the Romans in 455.
claims.note: Prosper of Aquitaine, who worked for Leo, records the meeting in his chronicle.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead, and the western empire has only 15 years left. Soon there will be no emperor in Rome at all, just Gothic kings on the doorstep and Greek ones far away.

reigns.title: Between Goths and Greeks
reigns.tagline: Emperors vanish, kings bully, and the plague arrives
reigns.previously: Leo the Great dies, the man who faced down Attila.
paragraphs: Within 15 years of Leo's death the western empire was gone. In 476 the general Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and didn't bother replacing him. Popes now dealt with barbarian kings in Italy and a Roman emperor far off in Constantinople. In 494 Gelasius I wrote to that emperor that the world was ruled by two powers, the sacred authority of bishops and royal power, and the bishops' was the weightier.

Theodoric the Ostrogoth ruled Italy fairly well until he turned on Rome. He sent Pope John I on a mission to Constantinople, disliked the result and threw him into prison at Ravenna, where he died in 526. Then Emperor Justinian sent armies to win Italy back. The war wrecked the country, and Justinian treated popes as his officials. He had Vigilius brought to Constantinople and leaned on him for years to sign off his theology.

In 568 the Lombards poured over the Alps and seized much of Italy, and Constantinople sent little help. Rome was hungry, flooded and frightened. In 590 plague swept the city, and Pope Pelagius II was one of the first to die.

claims.text: Gelasius told the emperor that priestly power outweighs royal power.
claims.note: His letter to Emperor Anastasius I survives, and medieval popes quoted it for centuries.

claims.text: Theodoric deliberately starved Pope John I to death.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis treats John as a martyr. How exactly he died in custody is unclear.

reigns.hook: Plague in the streets, Lombards in the countryside, and no pope. The Romans turn to a rich former official turned monk, who badly wants to say no.

reigns.tagline: The monk who fed Rome and sent a mission to England
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Deacon and envoy of Pelagius II
reigns.previously: Plague kills Pelagius II. The Lombards are closing in on Rome.
paragraphs: Gregory came from an old, rich Roman family and was prefect of the city, its top civil official, by his early thirties. Then he gave it all up. He turned his family's house on the Caelian Hill into a monastery and became a monk. Popes kept hauling him back out, first as a deacon, then as their envoy in Constantinople. In 590 the Romans chose him as pope. He tried to wriggle out of it, but the emperor confirmed the election.

He turned out to be brilliant at the job. With no help from Constantinople, he fed Rome from the Church's estates, paid soldiers and bargained with the Lombards himself. He wrote a handbook for bishops that was read for centuries. In 596 he sent the monk Augustine and a band of about 40 companions to convert the pagan English. Augustine baptised King Æthelberht of Kent and became the first archbishop of Canterbury.

Gregory called himself 'servant of the servants of God', a title popes still use. He was often ill with gout and stomach trouble, and he died in March 604. The Church counts him among the four great doctors of the Latin West.

claims.text: Seeing fair-haired English slave boys for sale in Rome, Gregory punned that they were angels, not Angles.
claims.note: Bede tells the story more than a century later, borrowing it from an earlier Life of Gregory written in England.

claims.text: Gregory composed or collected Gregorian chant.
claims.note: The chant took shape in the 8th and 9th centuries; the Franks credited it to Gregory to give it prestige.

claims.text: Gregory sent Augustine to England in 596.
claims.note: Gregory's own letters about the mission survive in his Register, and Bede copied several of them.

reigns.hook: Gregory leaves a city that runs on Church grain. For the next century and a half, popes will still need an emperor's say-so to take office, and Constantinople won't let them forget it.

reigns.title: The Byzantine Papacy
reigns.tagline: Popes on the emperor's leash, until they slip it
reigns.previously: Gregory the Great dies, having run Rome as well as its church.
paragraphs: For a century and a half after Gregory, a new pope could not be consecrated until the emperor in Constantinople approved, and the wait could take months. Doctrine was a minefield. Honorius I tried to calm a row about Christ's will with a vague formula. Decades after his death, the Council of Constantinople in 681 condemned him as a heretic, and later popes accepted the verdict.

Martin I refused to keep quiet about the same theology. In 653 Emperor Constans II had him arrested in Rome and shipped to Constantinople, where he was tried, humiliated and exiled to Crimea. He died there in 655. Meanwhile a run of popes from Greece, Syria and Sicily took the chair, many of them from families that had fled the Arab conquests.

Then the emperors started smashing religious images. Gregory II and Gregory III refused to go along with iconoclasm, and the bond with Constantinople frayed. The Lombards kept pushing towards Rome, so Pope Zachary looked north to the Franks. In 751 he backed the plan of Pepin the Short, the real power in Francia, to depose the last feeble Merovingian king and take the crown himself.

claims.text: A council condemned Pope Honorius I as a heretic.
claims.note: The acts of the Council of Constantinople (680 to 681) name him, and Pope Leo II confirmed it. Opponents of papal infallibility cited it in 1870.

claims.text: Martin I was tried in Constantinople and died in exile in Crimea.
claims.note: His own letters from captivity and a contemporary account of his trial survive.

claims.text: Zachary told the Franks that the man with real power should be king.
claims.note: The story comes from the Royal Frankish Annals, written decades later at the court of Pepin's family, which wanted papal approval on record.

reigns.hook: Zachary dies. The Lombard king is at Rome's door, and the emperor won't help. The next pope is about to do something no pope has ever done: cross the Alps.

reigns.tagline: The pope who crossed the Alps and came back with a state
reigns.previously: Zachary dies, having blessed Pepin's grab for the Frankish crown.
paragraphs: First, the numbering. After Zachary died, a priest named Stephen was elected but died of a stroke a few days later, before he could be consecrated. Some lists count him and some don't, so this pope turns up as Stephen II or Stephen III depending on the book. Within days the Romans picked a deacon, also called Stephen.

The Lombard king Aistulf had taken Ravenna and wanted Rome, and Constantinople sent nothing. So late in 753 Stephen did what no pope had done before: he crossed the Alps to the Frankish court. He met Pepin the Short in January 754. That summer at Saint-Denis he anointed Pepin king, along with his two young sons. One of them was the future Charlemagne.

Pepin paid him back. He marched into Italy and beat Aistulf twice, and in 756 handed the conquered lands, Ravenna and a band of territory across central Italy, to the pope instead of the emperor. This was the Donation of Pepin, the birth of the Papal States. The pope was now a ruler of land and people, and would stay one for 1,100 years. Stephen died in April 757.

claims.text: At their first meeting Pepin walked beside the pope's horse like a groom.
claims.note: The papal biography says so. Frankish sources instead have Stephen kneeling in sackcloth before Pepin. Each side told it its own way.

claims.text: Stephen was the first pope to cross the Alps.
claims.note: His journey is described in his life in the Liber Pontificalis and in Frankish annals.

claims.text: The forged Donation of Constantine was made in Rome around this time to back papal claims.
claims.note: Many historians date it to the mid or late 8th century, but exactly when, where and why it was forged is still argued.

reigns.hook: Stephen has a state. Now the Roman nobles want it, and one of them is about to make his brother pope, though the brother isn't even a priest.

reigns.title: Rome Turns West
reigns.tagline: A fake pope, a blinding, and a new best friend in the north
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Paul I was Stephen II's brother
reigns.previously: Stephen II dies, the first ruler of the new Papal States.
paragraphs: Stephen's brother Paul I took over and spent ten years holding off the Lombards and Constantinople with Frankish help. When he died in 767 the new papal state showed its ugly side. A nobleman, Duke Toto of Nepi, marched armed men into Rome and made his brother Constantine pope, though he was a layman. Constantine was rushed through holy orders in a matter of days.

A year later the papal officials struck back with Lombard help. Constantine was deposed and blinded, and Stephen III was elected. A synod in 769 ruled that laymen could never again be made pope. Then in 772 came Hadrian I, a Roman noble. When the Lombard king Desiderius threatened Rome, Hadrian called in Pepin's son, Charlemagne.

Charlemagne besieged Pavia and ended the Lombard kingdom in 774. That Easter he came to Rome and confirmed his father's grant of land to the pope. Hadrian reigned almost 24 years, a record that lasted a thousand years. When he died on Christmas Day 795, Charlemagne wept at the news.

claims.text: The usurper Constantine II was deposed and blinded.
claims.note: The Liber Pontificalis, written by the winning side, describes his downfall in grim detail, and the acts of the 769 synod survive.

claims.text: Charlemagne wept at Hadrian's death and sent an epitaph to Rome.
claims.note: Einhard, who knew Charlemagne, mentions the tears. The marble epitaph, with verses usually credited to Alcuin, survives at St Peter's.

reigns.hook: Hadrian's death leaves his powerful nephews out in the cold. The new pope comes from a humbler family, and they don't intend to put up with him for long.

reigns.tagline: The pope who made an emperor on Christmas Day
reigns.cameToPower: Elected the day after Hadrian died
reigns.previously: Hadrian I dies on Christmas Day. Charlemagne weeps for him.
paragraphs: Leo was a career churchman from an ordinary family, elected the day after Hadrian died. Hadrian's relatives held top jobs at the papal court and loathed him. On 25 April 799, as Leo rode in a procession through Rome, a gang led by Hadrian's nephew Paschal dragged him from his horse and tried to cut out his eyes and tongue. They locked him in a monastery, but he got away by night.

He fled north to Charlemagne at Paderborn. His enemies sent charges after him, including adultery and perjury. Charlemagne sent him home under escort and came to Rome himself late in 800. On 23 December, before an assembly in St Peter's, Leo swore on the Gospels that he was innocent. It was agreed that no one could sit in judgement on the pope.

Two days later, at Christmas Mass in St Peter's, Leo put a crown on Charlemagne's head and the crowd hailed him emperor of the Romans. The West had an emperor again for the first time in over 300 years, and a pope had crowned him. Leo outlived Charlemagne and died in June 816. He left a precedent popes would lean on for centuries: emperors got their crowns from Rome.

claims.text: His attackers did cut out his eyes and tongue, and God healed him by a miracle.
claims.note: Leo's supporters said so. Frankish sources say he was attacked; most historians think the mutilation simply failed.

claims.text: Charlemagne would never have entered the church that day had he known what the pope planned.
claims.note: Einhard says so. Historians argue whether Charlemagne was truly surprised or just disliked the pope taking the credit.

claims.text: Leo swore an oath of innocence two days before the coronation.
claims.note: Recorded in the Liber Pontificalis and the Frankish annals for 23 December 800.

reigns.hook: Leo and Charlemagne are both gone. The empire is splitting between squabbling heirs, and out at sea Arab raiders know exactly where Rome's richest church stands, outside the walls.

reigns.title: Raiders at the Gates
reigns.tagline: Pirates at St Peter's, forgers in the archives
reigns.previously: Leo III dies in 816, sixteen years after crowning Charlemagne.
paragraphs: In August 846 Arab raiders sailed up the Tiber. St Peter's and St Paul's stood outside the city walls, and the raiders stripped them of their treasure. Rome was shocked. The next pope, Leo IV, built a wall right round the Vatican hill so it would never happen again. That district is still called the Leonine City. In 849 a fleet from the south Italian ports beat another raiding force off Ostia, and Leo got the credit.

Then came Nicholas I, from 858 to 867, the toughest pope in centuries. He told kings what to do, forced a Frankish king to take back the wife he had tried to dump, and fell out badly with Photius, the new patriarch of Constantinople. Around the same time a set of brilliant forgeries appeared in Francia, the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. They put fake letters into the mouths of early popes, and they boosted papal power for centuries.

The end of the century turned nasty. John VIII spent his reign begging for help against the raiders and fighting Roman factions. In December 882 he became the first pope said to have been murdered by his own people. After him, short reigns followed, and the great Roman families began to circle the throne.

claims.text: In the 850s a woman, disguised as a man, reigned as Pope Joan until she gave birth during a procession.
claims.note: First told in the 13th century, about 400 years later. The record runs straight from Leo IV to Benedict III with no gap for her.

claims.text: John VIII was poisoned by a relative, then finished off with a hammer when the poison worked too slowly.
claims.note: Only the Annals of Fulda, written far away in Germany, tell the story. Nothing in Rome confirms or denies it.

claims.text: The Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals were forgeries.
claims.note: Made by Frankish clergy around the 840s to 850s. Doubts were raised in the 15th century and the fakes were fully exposed by the 17th.

reigns.hook: Stephen V is dead. The man the Romans pick next is an old bishop that John VIII once excommunicated. His name is Formosus, and even death won't save him from his enemies.

reigns.tagline: The pope whose troubles began after his funeral
reigns.previously: Stephen V dies. The dukes of Spoleto hold the imperial crown.
paragraphs: Formosus had a career before he had a throne. As bishop of Porto he was sent to Bulgaria in 866, and the Bulgarian ruler liked him so much he asked for him as archbishop. Rome said no. Then he made enemies. In 876 John VIII accused him of plotting and excommunicated him, and Formosus fled. A later pope lifted the ban, and in 891, already old, Formosus was elected pope himself.

Italy was a mess. The imperial title had fallen to Guy, duke of Spoleto, and Formosus crowned Guy's son Lambert as co-emperor in 892. But the Spoleto family leaned hard on Rome, so the pope wrote north to Arnulf, king of the East Franks. Arnulf marched into Italy, took Rome, and was crowned emperor by Formosus in February 896.

It went wrong at once. Arnulf fell ill and went home, and the Spoleto party was still there. Weeks later, on 4 April 896, Formosus died. He was buried in St Peter's. The Spoleto faction, and Lambert's fierce mother Ageltrude, had a long memory.

claims.text: The Bulgarian ruler Boris asked for Formosus as his archbishop.
claims.note: Papal letters and the Liber Pontificalis record the request and Rome's refusal.

claims.text: Formosus plotted against John VIII.
claims.note: The charges came from John VIII's camp in a time of bitter factions. Many historians think they were political.

claims.text: Arnulf was poisoned on Ageltrude's orders.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona tells it decades later. Arnulf probably had a stroke or similar illness.

reigns.hook: Formosus lies in his tomb in St Peter's. Nine months from now his enemies will dig him up, dress him in his robes and put him on trial.

reigns.title: The Cadaver Synod
reigns.tagline: The dead pope who was put on trial
reigns.previously: Formosus dies weeks after crowning Arnulf emperor.
paragraphs: Boniface VI lasted about two weeks. Then came Stephen VI, backed by the Spoleto faction. In January 897 he had Formosus's body, nine months dead, dug up, dressed in papal vestments and propped on a throne in the Lateran. A deacon stood beside the corpse to answer for it. Stephen screamed the charges himself. The verdict was guilty.

They stripped the body, cut off the three fingers Formosus had used to bless, and threw what was left into the Tiber. Every act of his reign was cancelled, including the priests and bishops he had ordained. Rome turned on Stephen. By the summer of 897 he was in prison, and there he was strangled.

Theodore II, who reigned about twenty days, gave Formosus a proper burial back in St Peter's. Popes came and went, six in seven years after Stephen's death. The last of them, Christopher, had locked up his predecessor. In January 904 he was thrown out and locked up in turn.

claims.text: A dead pope was put on trial in January 897, with a deacon speaking for him.
claims.note: Writers of the time, Formosus's defenders among them, describe it, and later synods condemned the trial.

claims.text: The Lateran basilica collapsed soon after, and people saw it as God's verdict.
claims.note: The basilica did fall around this time. The link to the trial comes from writers keen to see a sign.

claims.text: A monk pulled Formosus's body from the Tiber and hid it until it could be reburied.
claims.note: Told by later writers with miracles added, such as statues in St Peter's bowing to the corpse.

reigns.hook: The new pope is Sergius III, who sat on the bench at the Cadaver Synod. He has friends in a rich Roman family. Their women are about to become the most notorious in papal history.

reigns.title: The Pornocracy
reigns.tagline: When a mother and daughter ran the papacy
reigns.previously: Pope Christopher is thrown out and locked up in January 904.
paragraphs: Sergius III took the throne with armed help, and both his rivals died in prison. His backers were the family of Theophylact, a noble who ran the city's money and soldiers. Theophylact's wife Theodora and their daughter Marozia were the real power in Rome for a generation. The sources say Marozia, still a teenager, became Sergius's mistress and bore him a son.

John X was the strongest pope of the age. He helped lead the army that crushed a Saracen base on the Garigliano river in 915. But he crossed Marozia, and in 928 she had him thrown into prison, where he died. A few years later she made her own son pope, John XI.

Then her other son, Alberic, struck. At Marozia's wedding to the king of Italy in 932, he raised the Romans against them. The king fled over the walls and Marozia vanished into a cell. Alberic ruled Rome for over twenty years, and the popes of his day did as he said. Dying in 954, he made the Romans swear to elect his own son as the next pope.

claims.text: Marozia was Sergius III's mistress and the mother of his son, the future John XI.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona says so, and he loathed the Romans. A brief papal list also calls John XI Sergius's son, so many historians accept it.

claims.text: John X was smothered with a pillow in prison on Marozia's orders.
claims.note: Liutprand again. Other sources just say he died in custody.

claims.text: People at the time called this the Pornocracy.
claims.note: No. The label came from much later historians. Cardinal Baronius, around 1600, called the whole era the 'dark age', saeculum obscurum.

reigns.hook: Agapetus II is dead, and the Romans keep their oath to Alberic. The new pope is his son Octavian, about 18, who would rather hunt and party than pray.

reigns.tagline: The teenage pope who crowned an emperor, then crossed him
reigns.reignEnded: Died, said to be in a lover's bed
reigns.previously: Alberic dies. The Romans have sworn to make his son pope.
paragraphs: Octavian, son of Alberic II, was prince of Rome and then pope, taking the name John XII. He was about 18. His enemies said he gambled, hunted and kept a harem in the Lateran. When Berengar, king of Italy, threatened the papal lands, John called in Otto I of Germany. On 2 February 962 he crowned Otto emperor in St Peter's, and Otto promised to protect the pope's territory.

Almost at once John started plotting with Otto's enemies. Otto came back in late 963, and John fled with the papal treasure. Otto's synod in St Peter's put him on trial in his absence, and the charges were spectacular: perjury, murder, incest and toasting the devil. In December he was deposed and a layman, Leo VIII, was made pope in his place.

As soon as Otto's back was turned, John returned and took his revenge on the men who had judged him. One had his hand cut off, others were whipped or mutilated. Then, in May 964, John suddenly collapsed and died. He was about 27.

claims.text: John XII died after being struck down in bed with a married woman, by the devil or by her husband.
claims.note: Liutprand of Cremona, Otto's spokesman and John's enemy, says the devil struck him. The jealous husband appears in later retellings.

claims.text: The synod's charges, such as toasting the devil, were true.
claims.note: Our account comes from Liutprand, who wrote for Otto. Even so, few historians doubt John lived wildly.

claims.text: Otto I promised in writing to protect the pope's lands in 962.
claims.note: The Diploma Ottonianum survives in a fine copy in the Vatican archives.

reigns.hook: The Romans elect Benedict V; Otto carts him off to Germany. For the next eighty years emperors and Roman clans will make and break popes, and one young pope will try to sell the job.

reigns.title: A Papacy for Sale
reigns.tagline: Strangled popes, a wizard pope and one sold job
reigns.previously: John XII collapses and dies in May 964, aged about 27.
paragraphs: For eighty years the papacy was a prize fought over by German emperors and Roman noble clans, first the Crescentii and then the Counts of Tusculum. When the emperor was in Italy, his men got the job. When he left, the Romans struck back. Benedict VI was strangled in prison in 974 on the orders of a rival.

In 999 Otto III made his old tutor pope. Gerbert of Aurillac, now Sylvester II, was the first French pope and the cleverest man in Europe. He taught maths with an abacus and studied the stars. He was pope as the year 1000 came and went, and people later whispered that so much learning must have come from the devil.

Then the Tusculans turned the papacy into a family business. In 1032 they made a young nephew pope as Benedict IX. He was thrown out, came back, and in 1045 sold the office to his godfather, who became Gregory VI. By 1046 three men claimed to be pope. Emperor Henry III held a synod at Sutri that December and swept them all away.

claims.text: Sylvester II sold his soul to the devil in exchange for his learning and the papacy.
claims.note: Told by William of Malmesbury over a century later. A scholar who knew Arabic maths looked like a wizard to some.

claims.text: Benedict IX was only 12 when he became pope.
claims.note: Rodulfus Glaber hints he was a boy. Modern historians think he was probably about 20.

claims.text: Benedict IX sold the papacy to his godfather in 1045.
claims.note: The details vary, but sources agree that money changed hands and Gregory VI took over.

reigns.hook: Henry III wants a clean sweep. His candidate, a German bishop, is elected on Christmas Eve 1046 and crowns him emperor the next day. The reformers have arrived.

reigns.title: The Reformers
reigns.tagline: German popes, a schism and a power behind the throne
reigns.previously: Henry III clears out three rival popes at Sutri and picks his own.
paragraphs: Henry III's first pope, Clement II, was dead within a year. His successor lasted 23 days. Then came Leo IX, an Alsatian aristocrat and the emperor's cousin, who changed everything. He toured Europe holding councils, sacking bishops who had bought their jobs and attacking married priests. In 1053 he led an army against the Normans in southern Italy, lost at Civitate and spent months as their captive.

Leo died in April 1054. His legate in Constantinople, Cardinal Humbert, didn't let that stop him. On 16 July he marched into Hagia Sophia and laid a bull excommunicating the patriarch on the high altar. The patriarch excommunicated him back. It became the symbol of the split between Catholic and Orthodox churches.

Rome wanted popes free of emperors and Roman mobs. In 1059 Nicholas II gave the vote to the cardinals. Behind all this stood a short, fierce monk named Hildebrand, the archdeacon of Rome. In 1066 Alexander II blessed William of Normandy's invasion of England.

claims.text: Clement II was poisoned with lead.
claims.note: Tests on his remains in Bamberg in the 1950s found high lead levels. Murder or medicine? Nobody knows.

claims.text: Alexander II sent William of Normandy a papal banner for the invasion of 1066.
claims.note: William of Poitiers, the duke's own chaplain, says so. No papal record survives.

claims.text: The 1054 excommunications were personal, not a formal break between the churches.
claims.note: They named the patriarch and the legates. The split hardened over the next centuries; Paul VI and Athenagoras lifted them in 1965.

reigns.hook: April 1073. At Alexander II's funeral the crowd starts shouting a name. It belongs to the little archdeacon who has been running things for years.

reigns.tagline: The monk who made an emperor stand in the snow
reigns.previously: Alexander II dies. His archdeacon has run things for years.
paragraphs: Hildebrand was small, plain and fearless. The crowd at Alexander II's funeral demanded him, and the cardinals agreed. As Gregory VII he set out to free the Church from lay control. In his register sits a list of claims called the Dictatus Papae. Among them: the pope can be judged by no one, and the pope alone may depose emperors.

The clash came over who appointed bishops, the Investiture Controversy. The young German king Henry IV had his bishops declare Gregory deposed. Gregory excommunicated Henry, and the German princes began to desert their king. In January 1077 Henry crossed the Alps in winter and stood outside the castle of Canossa as a penitent until Gregory lifted the ban.

The peace didn't last. Gregory excommunicated Henry again in 1080, and Henry set up his own pope, Clement III. In 1084 Henry took Rome. Gregory's Norman allies under Robert Guiscard drove him out, then sacked the city. The Romans blamed the pope. Gregory left with the Normans and died at Salerno the next year.

claims.text: Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow at Canossa for three days.
claims.note: Gregory's own letter says three days in penance outside the gate. The barefoot details come from the chronicler Lampert, and both were on Gregory's side.

claims.text: His dying words were: 'I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile.'
claims.note: Reported by his admirers. It echoes Psalm 45, which makes it sound like a line polished afterwards.

claims.text: The Dictatus Papae was written in Gregory's papal register in 1075.
claims.note: The original register survives in the Vatican. Whether the list was ever published at the time is unclear.

reigns.hook: Gregory dies in exile, with Henry's pope sitting in Rome. His cardinals need someone with nerve. The first man they choose won't last long; the second will send an army to Jerusalem.

reigns.tagline: The pope who launched the First Crusade
reigns.previously: Victor III, abbot of Monte Cassino, lasts barely a year as pope.
paragraphs: After Gregory VII came Victor III, the abbot of Monte Cassino, who was ill and lasted only a year. Then the cardinals met at Terracina, south of Rome, because the antipope Clement III held the city. They chose Odo, a French nobleman, a former monk of Cluny and bishop of Ostia. He took the name Urban II. For years he could barely set foot in his own capital.

Urban was smoother than Gregory. He won friends, built alliances and slowly took back Rome. In March 1095 envoys from the Byzantine emperor came to his council at Piacenza asking for soldiers against the Turks. Urban had a bigger idea. On 27 November 1095, in a field outside Clermont in France, he called on the knights of the West to march east and free Jerusalem.

The response stunned everyone. Tens of thousands took the cross. After three brutal years the crusaders took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and slaughtered many of its people. Urban died in Rome two weeks later, on 29 July, before the news could reach him.

claims.text: The crowd at Clermont roared 'Deus vult!', 'God wills it!'
claims.note: Our versions of the speech were written years later by men such as Robert the Monk and Fulcher of Chartres, and they differ a lot.

claims.text: Urban died without learning that Jerusalem had fallen.
claims.note: He died on 29 July 1099, two weeks after the city fell. News took weeks to travel from Palestine to Rome.

claims.text: Urban promised crusaders full remission of the penance for their sins.
claims.note: A canon of the Council of Clermont says so, though exactly what was promised was soon inflated.

reigns.hook: The crusaders hold Jerusalem, but the man who sent them never knew. The new pope, Paschal II, will soon learn what Henry IV's son thinks of popes.

reigns.title: Concordats and Rival Popes
reigns.tagline: Kidnapped popes, double elections and one Englishman
reigns.previously: Urban II dies two weeks after his crusaders take Jerusalem.
paragraphs: The fight over who appoints bishops wasn't over. In 1111 Paschal II tried a bold deal with the German king Henry V, and it blew up in St Peter's itself. Henry seized the pope and his cardinals and held them until Paschal gave in and crowned him emperor. It took until 1122 and the Concordat of Worms for Callixtus II to settle it: the Church chose bishops, the emperor got to watch and hand over the lands.

Then the cardinals split. In 1130 two rival factions elected Innocent II and Anacletus II on the same day. The abbot Bernard of Clairvaux, the loudest voice in Europe, backed Innocent and toured the courts until the kings agreed. Meanwhile the Romans rose up, set up their own commune and senate in 1144, and fought the popes in the streets. Eugene III, a monk Bernard had trained, preached the Second Crusade, which fizzled out at Damascus in 1148.

In 1154 came the only English pope, Nicholas Breakspear, as Adrian IV. He put all Rome under interdict to force out the radical preacher Arnold of Brescia, who was handed over and executed in 1155. Adrian crowned Frederick Barbarossa that same year, but the two soon fell out over whether the empire was a gift from the pope. Adrian died at Anagni in September 1159.

claims.text: Lucius II died after being struck by a stone while leading an attack on the rebel senate on the Capitol in 1145.
claims.note: The stone comes from chroniclers writing later; other accounts say only that he died soon after the failed assault.

claims.text: Adrian IV's bull Laudabiliter granted Ireland to Henry II of England.
claims.note: The text survives only through Gerald of Wales, an interested party. Historians still argue whether it is genuine, doctored or invented.

claims.text: Adrian IV choked to death on a fly that flew into his wine.
claims.note: A tale told by hostile and later writers; contemporary accounts point to a throat illness, probably quinsy.

reigns.hook: Adrian is dead, and the cardinals are hopelessly split. When they meet to replace him, the election turns into a brawl over a scarlet cloak.

reigns.tagline: The pope who outlasted Barbarossa and four antipopes
reigns.previously: Adrian IV, the English pope, dies at Anagni, at odds with Barbarossa.
paragraphs: Rolando of Siena was a lawyer and the papal chancellor, and Frederick Barbarossa already hated him. At a meeting at Besançon in 1157 he had brought a letter from Adrian suggesting the empire was a papal gift, and a German noble nearly cut him down. When most cardinals chose Rolando in 1159, a minority chose Cardinal Octavian as Victor IV. The emperor backed Victor, and the Church had two popes again.

The schism lasted 18 years and Alexander spent much of it far from Rome, three years of it in France. Barbarossa kept naming new antipopes. But the cities of northern Italy formed the Lombard League against the emperor, and even named a new town Alessandria after the pope. In 1176 the League's foot soldiers beat Barbarossa at Legnano. In Venice in July 1177 the emperor knelt and kissed the pope's feet.

England gave him a crisis too. In 1170 Henry II's knights murdered Archbishop Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral. Alexander made Becket a saint in 1173, and Henry did public penance. In 1179 the Third Lateran Council ruled that a pope needs a two-thirds majority of the cardinals, which is still the rule. Alexander died in 1181, still unable to live safely in Rome.

claims.text: Octavian tore the scarlet papal mantle off Rolando and put it on himself, back to front in his haste.
claims.note: The vivid version comes from Alexander's own side, notably his biographer Cardinal Boso. Victor's supporters told a different story.

claims.text: Barbarossa prostrated himself and kissed the pope's feet at Venice in 1177.
claims.note: Described by eyewitnesses including Romuald of Salerno. The story that Alexander put his foot on the emperor's neck is a later legend.

claims.text: The two-thirds rule for electing a pope dates from Alexander's council of 1179.
claims.note: The decree Licet de vitanda of the Third Lateran Council. Popes have tinkered with it since, but it stands.

reigns.hook: Alexander is gone. Six years later Saladin takes Jerusalem, and Rome is waiting for a pope strong enough to make Christendom answer.

reigns.tagline: The most powerful pope of the Middle Ages
reigns.cameToPower: Elected the day Celestine III died
reigns.previously: Saladin takes Jerusalem in 1187, and old Celestine III dies in 1198.
paragraphs: Lotario dei Conti was a young noble trained in theology at Paris and law at Bologna. Elected at just 37, he believed the pope was Christ's vicar, set over kings as the sun is over the moon. He meant it. He took back control of the Papal States, ruled on disputed German elections, and turned kings into vassals.

His crusades went wild. The Fourth Crusade was meant for Egypt, but the crusaders sacked the Christian city of Zara and then, in April 1204, Constantinople itself, against his orders. In 1209 he launched a crusade against the Cathar heretics in southern France, which became a bloodbath. He put England under interdict in a fight with King John, who caved in 1213 and made England a papal fief. Two years later Innocent annulled Magna Carta.

He also saw what was new. In 1209 or 1210 he gave his blessing to a scruffy band from Assisi led by Francis. In 1215 he gathered more than 400 bishops at the Fourth Lateran Council, which ordered every Catholic to confess yearly and made Jews wear distinctive dress. He died suddenly at Perugia in July 1216, planning yet another crusade.

claims.text: Innocent dreamed that the Lateran basilica was falling and a small poor man held it up, and recognised Francis as that man.
claims.note: Told in the lives of Francis written decades later, notably by Bonaventure. It is a pious story, not a record.

claims.text: On the night he died, thieves stripped his body almost naked as it lay in the church at Perugia.
claims.note: Jacques de Vitry, who arrived in Perugia that week, says he saw it himself. It is a single witness, but a credible one.

claims.text: Urban III died of grief on hearing that Jerusalem had fallen in 1187.
claims.note: Told by later chroniclers. Urban died at Ferrara in October 1187, weeks after the fall; any grief may have been for the defeat at Hattin.

reigns.hook: Innocent is dead. His former ward, Frederick II, now rules Sicily and Germany, and he has no intention of being anyone's vassal.

reigns.title: Popes, Staufer and the Longest Conclave
reigns.tagline: A war with an emperor, then a pope who quit
reigns.previously: Innocent III dies at Perugia, his body stripped by thieves.
paragraphs: For decades the popes fought the Staufer emperor Frederick II, who ruled Sicily below the Papal States and Germany above them. Gregory IX excommunicated him twice and in 1231 set up the papal Inquisition to hunt heretics. Innocent IV fled to Lyon and had a council depose Frederick in 1245. Frederick died in 1250, but the popes went after his heirs. Clement IV invited Charles of Anjou to take Sicily, and young Conradin, the last Staufer, was beheaded at Naples in 1268.

Then the cardinals at Viterbo couldn't agree. The vacancy ran from November 1268 to September 1271, nearly three years. They finally chose a man who wasn't even a cardinal and was away on crusade at Acre: Gregory X. He brought in strict rules in 1274 to lock cardinals in until they chose. That was the start of the conclave as we know it.

In 1294, after another two-year deadlock, the cardinals chose a hermit in his eighties, Pietro da Morrone, as Celestine V. He was holy, and hopeless. Charles II of Naples ran him, and favours were handed out wildly. After five months he asked whether a pope could resign, was told yes, and did it on 13 December 1294.

claims.text: The people of Viterbo locked the cardinals in, cut their food to bread and water, and tore the roof off the palace.
claims.note: The lock-in and rationing are well attested. The roof story is widely told, though some historians think it was smaller-scale or later embroidered.

claims.text: Dante's soul in Limbo who made 'the great refusal' out of cowardice is Celestine V.
claims.note: Dante never names him in Inferno 3. Early commentators mostly said Celestine; others suggest Pontius Pilate or Esau.

reigns.hook: The hermit is free to go home to his mountain. Or so he thinks. The cardinal who advised him on resigning is about to become pope, and wants no rival on the loose.

reigns.tagline: The proudest pope, and the slap that broke him
reigns.previously: The hermit pope Celestine V resigns after five months.
paragraphs: Benedetto Caetani was a brilliant canon lawyer from Anagni, and he had helped Celestine find the legal way out. Elected eleven days later, he wasn't taking chances. Celestine was caught trying to flee and locked up in the castle of Fumone, where he died in 1296. Boniface moved the court back to Rome, made war on the Colonna clan, who said his election was invalid, and razed their town of Palestrina.

In 1300 he declared the first Jubilee, and pilgrims poured into Rome for the pardon he offered. But he picked a fight he couldn't win. Philip IV of France wanted to tax his clergy. Boniface forbade it, and in 1302 issued Unam Sanctam: every human being must be subject to the pope to be saved.

Philip's answer was force. On 7 September 1303 his minister Guillaume de Nogaret and Sciarra Colonna burst into the papal palace at Anagni and seized the old man. The townspeople freed him after a few days, but he was broken. He went back to Rome and died a month later. Dante had already saved him a place in hell.

claims.text: Sciarra Colonna slapped the pope in the face with an iron gauntlet at Anagni.
claims.note: The famous 'slap of Anagni' isn't in the earliest reports, which describe threats and insults. It grew in the telling.

claims.text: Dante put Boniface in hell while he was still alive.
claims.note: Inferno is set in 1300, so Dante has Pope Nicholas III, in the pit of the simoniacs (canto 19), expecting Boniface to arrive.

claims.text: Boniface was a heretic and a blasphemer who didn't believe in the afterlife.
claims.note: Charges made by Philip IV's lawyers in a posthumous trial they pushed for years. Political smears, never proved.

reigns.hook: Boniface is dead, and the French king has won. Within two years the cardinals choose a Frenchman, and he will never set foot in Rome.

reigns.title: The Avignon Papacy
reigns.tagline: Seven French popes and a palace on the Rhône
reigns.previously: Boniface's successor, Benedict XI, dies suddenly after eight months.
paragraphs: After almost a year of deadlock, the cardinals chose an outsider: Bertrand de Got, archbishop of Bordeaux, as Clement V. He was crowned at Lyon, never went to Rome, and from 1309 settled at Avignon, a town on the Rhône next to papal land. He bent to Philip IV, dissolving the Knights Templar in 1312 after the king had them arrested and tortured. Their last grand master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in Paris in 1314.

For nearly 70 years the popes stayed. All seven were French, and so were most cardinals. John XXII built a superb tax machine and left a huge fortune. Benedict XII began the Palace of the Popes and Clement VI turned it into a showpiece, bought Avignon outright in 1348, and stayed put through the Black Death. Italians were furious. The poet Petrarch called it the Babylonian captivity, and wrote furious letters about the luxury of the papal court.

Urban V went back to Rome in 1367 but gave up after three years. Then Catherine of Siena, a young mystic, wrote and came in person to urge Gregory XI home. He sailed for Italy and entered Rome on 17 January 1377. Just over a year later, on 27 March 1378, he died there.

claims.text: Burning at the stake, Jacques de Molay summoned Clement V and Philip IV to God's judgement within the year, and both died within months.
claims.note: Pope and king did die in 1314, but the curse first appears in later chroniclers. It looks written after the fact.

claims.text: Benedict XI was poisoned with figs.
claims.note: Rumours spread at once and blamed several parties, including the French. There is no proof; dysentery is just as likely.

claims.text: Clement VI survived the plague by sitting between two great fires on his doctor's advice.
claims.note: Often linked to his physician Guy de Chauliac, but the evidence is thin and the story is mostly told later.

reigns.hook: For the first time in decades, the cardinals must hold a conclave in Rome. Outside, a mob is shouting for a Roman pope, or at least an Italian one.

reigns.title: The Western Schism
reigns.tagline: Two popes, then three, and a council to sack them all
reigns.previously: Gregory XI brings the papacy back to Rome, then dies there.
paragraphs: With a mob outside, the cardinals chose an Italian, the archbishop of Bari, as Urban VI. He soon turned on them with such rage that they fled, declared the election forced, and in September 1378 chose Robert of Geneva as Clement VII. He went back to Avignon. Now there were two popes, each with his own cardinals, and Europe picked by politics: France, Scotland and Spain mostly for Avignon; England, the Empire and much of Italy for Rome.

Each line kept electing successors. Rome had Boniface IX, Innocent VII and Gregory XII; Avignon had the stubborn Aragonese Benedict XIII. In 1409 the Council of Pisa deposed both and elected Alexander V, then John XXIII. Now there were three. In 1414 the German king Sigismund pushed for the Council of Constance. It deposed John XXIII, took Gregory XII's resignation on 4 July 1415 and deposed Benedict XIII, who held out at Peñíscola in Spain until he died.

On 11 November 1417 the council elected Martin V, and the schism was over. The Catholic Church today counts the Roman line, from Urban VI to Gregory XII, as the true popes, though that was only settled long afterwards. Gregory's resignation was the last until 2013. The name John XXIII came back in 1958.

claims.text: Urban VI had cardinals he suspected of plotting tortured, and five of them vanished, probably murdered.
claims.note: The torture is reported by contemporaries, including Dietrich of Nieheim, who was there. The fate of the five was never established.

claims.text: The Roman mob at the 1378 conclave shouted that they wanted a Roman, or at least an Italian.
claims.note: Reported on all sides; the rebel cardinals later used the threat of violence to argue the election was invalid.

claims.text: John XXIII fled Constance in disguise, dressed as a groom.
claims.note: He did slip away in March 1415 with help from Duke Frederick of Austria; the details of the disguise vary between chroniclers.

reigns.hook: Martin V is the one pope everyone can accept. He's a Colonna, a Roman, and he's heading home to a city half in ruins.

reigns.title: Back to Rome
reigns.tagline: Rebuilding a ruin, losing Constantinople, chasing comets
reigns.previously: The Council of Constance ends the schism and elects Martin V.
paragraphs: Martin V, Oddone Colonna, reached Rome in 1420 and found it shabby, half empty and full of ruins. He started repairing churches and walls and rebuilt papal power. His successor Eugene IV had a rougher time. A revolt drove him out of Rome in 1434, and the Council of Basel tried to run the Church without him. Eugene won by stealing its best card: at Florence in 1439 he signed a union with the Greek Church, whose emperor came begging help against the Turks.

The union collapsed back east, and on 29 May 1453 Constantinople fell to the Ottomans. Nicholas V, a book-loving scholar, founded the Vatican Library and dreamed of rebuilding St Peter's. Then came Calixtus III, the first Borgia pope, an old Spaniard who poured money into a crusade and brought his nephews to Rome.

Pius II, the humanist Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, wrote racy stories in his youth and frank memoirs as pope, the Commentaries. He took the cross himself and went to Ancona to lead a crusade, but the fleet barely came and he died there in August 1464. The Venetian Paul II loved carnival and jewels, and died suddenly in July 1471.

claims.text: Calixtus III excommunicated Halley's comet in 1456.
claims.note: The story grows out of Platina's account of prayers ordered against the comet and the Turks. No bull against a comet exists.

claims.text: Eugene IV escaped Rome in 1434 disguised as a monk, rowed down the Tiber under a shower of stones.
claims.note: Reported by contemporaries, but the details of the disguise and the boat vary from account to account.

claims.text: Paul II died of a stroke after eating two large melons.
claims.note: A story passed on by Platina, who had been jailed and tortured by Paul and hated him.

reigns.hook: Paul II is dead. The cardinals turn to a Franciscan friar from Liguria, who comes with a large crop of ambitious nephews.

reigns.tagline: The Franciscan who built a chapel and a family empire
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; a cardinal Paul II made
reigns.previously: Paul II dies suddenly. The cardinals meet in the summer heat.
paragraphs: Francesco della Rovere came from a modest family on the Ligurian coast and became a star Franciscan preacher and head of his order. As pope he took the name Sixtus, and he turned out to be a builder. He threw the Ponte Sisto across the Tiber for the Jubilee of 1475, reopened the Vatican Library to scholars and put up a big new chapel in the Vatican. It still carries his name: the Sistine.

He also looked after his family like no pope before him. Nephews became cardinals, lords and generals. That's where the word nepotism comes from: nipote, nephew. One nephew, Girolamo Riario, wanted Florence, and on 26 April 1478 his allies the Pazzi struck at Mass in Florence cathedral. Giuliano de' Medici was stabbed to death. His brother Lorenzo got away bleeding, and Florence hanged the plotters, an archbishop among them.

Sixtus answered by excommunicating Lorenzo and going to war with Florence. The same year he let Ferdinand and Isabella set up their own Inquisition in Spain. He died in August 1484, leaving the Sistine walls freshly painted by Botticelli, Perugino and Ghirlandaio, and a College of Cardinals stuffed with his relatives.

claims.text: Sixtus knew about the plot to kill the Medici brothers in the cathedral.
claims.note: The hired soldier Montesecco confessed that Sixtus wanted the Medici gone but said no one should die. Historians still argue over how much he knew.

claims.text: The Sistine Chapel is named after Sixtus IV.
claims.note: He built it in the 1470s and early 1480s; the name comes from Sisto, Italian for Sixtus.

claims.text: The word nepotism comes from popes promoting their nephews.
claims.note: It comes from the Italian nipote, nephew. Sixtus is the classic example, though plenty of popes before and after did the same.

reigns.hook: Next comes Innocent VIII, then a Spanish cardinal who has served as the Church's vice-chancellor for 35 years. He knows every cardinal's price.

reigns.tagline: The Borgia pope and the family that shocked Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Won a conclave said to be bought
reigns.previously: Innocent VIII, the first pope to own his children openly, is dead.
paragraphs: Rodrigo Borgia was a Spaniard from Valencia and the nephew of Pope Calixtus III, who made him a cardinal young. He ran the papal chancery for decades and grew very rich. In August 1492 he was elected pope. Rome buzzed with talk that he had bought the votes with mule-loads of silver. He was clever, charming and tireless, and he made no secret of his children.

His mistress Vannozza dei Cattanei had given him Cesare, Juan, Lucrezia and Jofré. In 1493 his bull Inter caetera split the newly found lands across the Atlantic between Spain and Portugal. In 1494 Charles VIII of France marched through Italy and into Rome. In 1497 Juan was murdered and his body fished out of the Tiber. A year later the preacher Savonarola, who had denounced Alexander, was hanged and burned in Florence.

Cesare left the Church and carved out a state for the family in the Romagna, with his father's money and troops. Then in August 1503 father and son both fell ill after a dinner. Cesare survived. Alexander died, and his body swelled so badly it had to be forced into its coffin. Rome said poison. With the pope gone, Cesare's power crumbled.

claims.text: Rodrigo Borgia bought the papacy with bribes to the cardinals.
claims.note: Diplomats and chroniclers said so at the time, and gifts to cardinals did follow his election. Simony was common, so how decisive it was is argued.

claims.text: The Banquet of Chestnuts: an orgy in the Vatican in October 1501, watched by the pope and his children.
claims.note: It comes from the diary of Johann Burchard, the papal master of ceremonies, but may be gossip he wrote down. Many historians doubt it.

claims.text: Alexander was poisoned, perhaps by a cup meant for someone else.
claims.note: The rumour was everywhere. But it was a deadly malaria season in Rome, and fever is the likelier cause.

reigns.hook: The Borgia is dead. His successor lasts 26 days. Now the man who spent years in exile hating Alexander finally gets his chance, and he wants an army.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Nephew of Sixtus IV; Borgia's foe

reigns.previously: Alexander VI is dead, and Pius III lasts just 26 days.
paragraphs: Giuliano della Rovere owed his red hat to his uncle Sixtus IV. He spent the Borgia years in exile in France, plotting. Elected pope in a single day in 1503, he took a name many heard as a nod to Julius Caesar, and he lived up to it. He wanted the Papal States back under Rome's control, and in 1506 he rode out at the head of his army and took Perugia and Bologna.

That same year 150 Swiss soldiers marched into Rome as his guard; their successors are still there. On 18 April 1506 he laid the first stone of a new St Peter's, to Bramante's design. He put Raphael to work on his rooms and talked Michelangelo into painting the Sistine ceiling, which took four years and a lot of shouting on both sides. It was unveiled in 1512.

His wars were a tangle of shifting alliances, first against Venice, then against France. During the fight over Bologna, which he lost again in 1511, he grew a beard and swore not to shave until the French were out of Italy. Raphael painted him like that, old and brooding. The French were pushed out in 1512, and Julius died in February 1513.

claims.text: Julius beat Michelangelo with a stick during one of their rows.
claims.note: The story comes from Ascanio Condivi's life of Michelangelo, written with the artist's help decades later.

claims.text: Erasmus wrote 'Julius Excluded from Heaven', a satire in which St Peter turns the pope away.
claims.note: It circulated anonymously from 1514. Erasmus always dodged the question; most scholars think it was his.

claims.text: The Swiss Guard first arrived in Rome on 22 January 1506.
claims.note: A company of about 150 Swiss reached Rome that day; the date is kept as the guard's founding day.

reigns.hook: The warrior is dead. The cardinals pick a 37-year-old Medici who isn't even a priest yet, and he has very different ideas about how to enjoy the job.

reigns.tagline: The Medici pope who spent lavishly and met Luther
reigns.previously: Julius II, the warrior pope, has died with the French driven out.
paragraphs: Giovanni de' Medici was the son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, and his father got him made a cardinal at 13. When he was elected pope in March 1513 he was only a deacon, so he was ordained priest and bishop in the days that followed. He loved music, hunting, theatre and jokes, and he spent money as fast as the Church could raise it.

Portugal sent him a white elephant called Hanno, who paraded through Rome and became a pet. To pay for the new St Peter's, Leo backed a sale of indulgences. In Germany it was preached hard, and on 31 October 1517 a friar called Martin Luther sent off 95 theses against it. Leo was slow to take him seriously. He finally excommunicated Luther in January 1521.

That October he named Henry VIII 'Defender of the Faith' for a book attacking Luther. Then in December 1521 he fell ill with a fever and died within days, aged 45. He left huge debts and a Church starting to crack in two.

claims.text: Leo said: 'God has given us the papacy, let us enjoy it.'
claims.note: It comes second-hand, in a Venetian ambassador's report of what Leo supposedly told his brother Giuliano.

claims.text: Leo was not yet a priest when he was elected pope.
claims.note: He was ordained priest on 15 March 1513, after the election.

claims.text: Leo was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours flew, as they did for many Renaissance popes. There was no proof, and a malarial fever is more likely.

reigns.hook: Leo is dead and Luther is winning. The cardinals pick a strict Dutch scholar who knows Rome is rotten. The Romans can't stand him.

reigns.tagline: The pope who watched Rome burn from a castle
reigns.previously: Adrian VI, the stern Dutch reformer, dies after 20 months.
paragraphs: Adrian VI, Charles V's old tutor, tried to clean up Rome and was mocked for it. He was the last non-Italian pope for 455 years. Next came Giulio de' Medici, born a month after his father Giuliano was killed in the Pazzi plot. Cousin Leo had made him a cardinal. He was a good administrator but, as pope, couldn't pick a side between France and the Emperor, so he picked both, one after the other.

It went horribly wrong. On 6 May 1527 an unpaid imperial army stormed Rome. The Swiss Guard died fighting on the steps of St Peter's while Clement ran along the raised passage to Castel Sant'Angelo. Rome was looted for months, and the pope was a prisoner until December. He grew a beard in mourning. In 1530 he made peace and crowned Charles V emperor at Bologna.

Meanwhile Henry VIII wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Charles V's aunt, annulled. Clement stalled for years and would not give it. England began breaking from Rome. Near the end he asked Michelangelo to paint the Last Judgement in the Sistine Chapel. He died in September 1534.

claims.text: 147 of the Swiss Guard were killed defending the pope on 6 May 1527.
claims.note: The figure is the guard's own tradition and is widely accepted; about 40 survived and escorted Clement to safety.

claims.text: Clement slipped out of Castel Sant'Angelo disguised as a servant.
claims.note: Several accounts say he escaped in disguise in December 1527, but his release had been negotiated, and the details vary.

claims.text: Clement was poisoned by eating death cap mushrooms.
claims.note: A rumour at the time. He had been ill for months, and nothing supports it.

reigns.hook: Clement is dead and England is lost. The cardinals turn to a 66-year-old who got his first red hat from the Borgia pope, some say thanks to his sister.

reigns.tagline: A Borgia-era playboy who launched the fight back
reigns.previously: Clement VII is dead. Rome was sacked and England is lost.
paragraphs: Alessandro Farnese was the ultimate Renaissance insider. Alexander VI made him a cardinal in 1493, and gossips said that was thanks to his beautiful sister Giulia, the Borgia pope's mistress. He had children before he became a priest. Within weeks of becoming pope he made two teenage grandsons cardinals, and he later carved the duchy of Parma out of the Papal States for his son Pier Luigi.

Yet this old-style pope started the fight back against Protestantism. He named serious reformers as cardinals. In 1540 he approved a new order, Ignatius of Loyola's Society of Jesus. In 1542 he set up the Roman Inquisition. And in December 1545 the long-awaited council finally opened at Trent.

Rome looked up too. Michelangelo's Last Judgement was unveiled in 1541, and in 1547 the old artist took charge of St Peter's. Titian painted Paul as a sharp, hunched old man. He died in November 1549, worn out and furious with his grandson Ottavio, who had defied him over Parma.

claims.text: Romans called him 'the petticoat cardinal' because his sister Giulia won him his red hat.
claims.note: It was a nickname of the time. Giulia was close to Alexander VI, but Alessandro was able and well connected on his own.

claims.text: Paul III approved the Jesuits in 1540.
claims.note: The bull Regimini militantis ecclesiae of 27 September 1540 founded the Society of Jesus.

claims.text: His final illness was brought on by rage at his grandson's betrayal.
claims.note: Contemporaries told it that way; he was 81 and fever was enough.

reigns.hook: The council at Trent is stuck, and Protestant Europe is growing. The next popes will be harder men: one of them is a fierce old inquisitor who will put Rome's Jews behind walls.

reigns.title: The Counter-Reformation
reigns.tagline: Ghettos, an Index of books and a great sea battle
reigns.previously: Paul III dies, and the council at Trent is stuck.
paragraphs: Julius III reopened Trent but enjoyed his villa more. Marcellus II, a real reformer, died after 22 days. Then came Paul IV Carafa, a fierce old inquisitor. In 1555 he walled Rome's Jews into a ghetto and made them wear yellow hats. In 1559 he issued the first Index of Forbidden Books. When he died that summer, Romans stormed the Inquisition's jail and knocked the head off his statue.

Pius IV, smoother and wiser, brought Trent to a close in December 1563. Its decrees shaped Catholic life for 400 years: seminaries for priests, a fixed catechism, bishops who actually lived in their dioceses. Then came Pius V, a Dominican inquisitor who kept wearing his friar's habit. In 1570 he excommunicated Elizabeth I of England and told her subjects not to obey her.

He also pulled Spain and Venice into a Holy League against the Ottomans. On 7 October 1571 its fleet smashed the Turkish navy at Lepanto, off Greece. Pius died the next spring and was later made a saint.

claims.text: Palestrina's Mass for Pope Marcellus convinced the Council of Trent not to ban polyphonic church music.
claims.note: The story grew up decades later. Trent did discuss music, but there is no evidence this Mass changed anyone's mind.

claims.text: Popes wear white because Pius V kept his white Dominican habit.
claims.note: A popular explanation, but popes wore white long before him. He may have fixed the custom.

claims.text: Romans toppled and beheaded Paul IV's statue when he died in 1559.
claims.note: Rioters broke into the Inquisition's prison and smashed his statue on the Capitol; the head was rolled through the streets.

reigns.hook: Pius V is dead. The next pope is a lawyer from Bologna with a son born before he was ordained. He will change the date on every calendar in the Catholic world.

reigns.tagline: The pope who deleted ten days
reigns.previously: Pius V, the saintly inquisitor of Lepanto, has died.
paragraphs: Ugo Boncompagni was a law professor from Bologna who had worked at Trent. Before he was ordained he had a son, Giacomo, whom he later made governor of Castel Sant'Angelo. In August 1572, three months into his reign, news came of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of Protestants in Paris. Gregory had a Te Deum sung and a medal struck to celebrate it.

His big legacy was time itself. The old Julian calendar had drifted ten days out against the sun, which threw off Easter. Astronomers worked out a fix, and Gregory's bull of February 1582 ordered it. In Catholic lands Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October. Protestants dragged their feet: Britain waited until 1752, and Russia until 1918.

He poured money into colleges for training priests, including the Jesuits' Roman College, now the Gregorian University. To pay for it he seized land from nobles, and bandits overran the Papal States. In March 1585 he welcomed four young Japanese envoys to Rome, and he died weeks later.

claims.text: Gregory celebrated the St Bartholomew's Day massacre with a Te Deum and a medal.
claims.note: The medal survives, showing an angel striking down the Huguenots, and Vasari painted the massacre in the Vatican's Sala Regia.

claims.text: Ten days simply vanished from the calendar in October 1582.
claims.note: Spain, Portugal, Poland and the Papal States switched at once; France followed in December.

claims.text: Rioters demanded 'Give us our eleven days!' when Britain switched in 1752.
claims.note: Based on a Hogarth print. Historians have found no real evidence of calendar riots.

reigns.hook: Gregory is dead and bandits rule the roads. The cardinals elect a farmer's son who is said to have herded pigs as a boy. He'll have heads on the bridges within months.

reigns.tagline: The swineherd pope who rebuilt Rome in five years
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; out of favour under Gregory
reigns.previously: Gregory XIII is dead. Bandits rule the roads of the Papal States.
paragraphs: Felice Peretti came from a poor family in the Marche and joined the Franciscans as a boy. As Cardinal Montalto he kept his head down under Gregory XIII. As pope he was a whirlwind. He went after the bandits without mercy, and the heads of the executed were stuck up on the Ponte Sant'Angelo. Within two years the roads were safe and the treasury full.

Then he rebuilt Rome. He drove long straight streets between the great churches, and he brought water back to the hills with a new aqueduct, the Acqua Felice. In 1586 his engineer Domenico Fontana moved the huge Egyptian obelisk to the front of St Peter's, using hundreds of men and horses. In 1590 the dome of St Peter's was finally closed.

He also fixed the number of cardinals at 70 and reorganised the Curia into departments. But he rushed out his own edition of the Latin Bible, and it was full of mistakes. He died in August 1590, and the Romans, who had hated his taxes, tried to pull down his statue.

claims.text: He hobbled into the conclave on a crutch, pretending to be feeble, and threw it away once elected.
claims.note: The tale comes from Gregorio Leti's lively 17th-century biography, which is full of inventions.

claims.text: 'Water on the ropes!': a sailor broke the order of silence to save the obelisk when its ropes began to burn.
claims.note: A much-loved Roman tale, written down long after the event.

claims.text: Sixtus's Vulgate Bible was so full of errors that it was recalled after his death.
claims.note: Copies were called in and a corrected edition, the Clementine Vulgate, came out in 1592.

reigns.hook: Sixtus is dead. The next pope bans smoking in church and dies of malaria before he's even crowned. Rome is in for a run of very short reigns.

reigns.title: Fire and Façades
reigns.tagline: A heretic burned, a dome finished, Galileo warned
reigns.previously: Sixtus V, the builder, dies hated by the Romans.
paragraphs: Urban VII lasted 13 days, the shortest reign of any pope, and died of malaria before he was crowned. Gregory XIV and Innocent IX were both dead by the end of 1591. Then came Clement VIII, who absolved Henry IV of France in 1595 and took Ferrara into the Papal States in 1598. His Rome was harsh: in 1599 young Beatrice Cenci was beheaded for her father's murder, and on 17 February 1600 the philosopher Giordano Bruno was burned alive in the Campo de' Fiori.

Paul V Borghese finished the long nave and the façade of St Peter's, and put his own name in giant letters across the front, where it still is. His nephew Cardinal Scipione built the Villa Borghese. In 1616 the Church declared that the Earth going round the sun was against Scripture, and Galileo was warned not to hold or defend it.
Gregory XV was pope for just two years, but he brought in the secret written ballot for conclaves and in 1622 set up Propaganda Fide to run missions around the world. He died in July 1623.

claims.text: Urban VII issued the world's first known ban on smoking, threatening excommunication for using tobacco in or near churches.
claims.note: Often repeated in histories of smoking. The better-documented papal tobacco bans came later, under Urban VIII (1624) and Innocent X.

claims.text: Giordano Bruno was burned in the Campo de' Fiori on 17 February 1600.
claims.note: Records of his trial and execution survive; a statue put up in 1889 marks the spot.

claims.text: Galileo was formally ordered never to teach Copernicanism 'in any way whatever' in 1616.
claims.note: An unsigned note in the file says so, but Cardinal Bellarmine's certificate for Galileo records only a warning. The difference mattered at his trial in 1633.

reigns.hook: The new pope is a poet and a Barberini, and he has long admired Galileo. Galileo thinks his moment has come.

reigns.tagline: The poet pope who put Galileo on trial
reigns.previously: Gregory XV dies, and the cardinals meet in the summer heat of 1623.
paragraphs: Maffeo Barberini was a Florentine diplomat who wrote Latin verse and liked clever company. As a cardinal he even wrote a poem in praise of Galileo. As pope he spent like a prince. Bernini built a giant bronze canopy over St Peter's tomb, and bronze was stripped from the porch of the ancient Pantheon. Most of that metal ended up as cannon for Castel Sant'Angelo.

Then Galileo published his Dialogue in 1632. It argued for a Sun-centred universe and gave one of the pope's favourite arguments to a character called Simplicio. Urban was furious. In 1633 the Inquisition made the old scientist kneel and renounce the idea that the Earth moves. Galileo spent his last years under house arrest near Florence.

Meanwhile the pope's nephews grew rich on Church money. Their feud with the Farnese family dragged the Papal States into the War of Castro, which ended in 1644 in a costly flop. When Urban died that July, many Romans openly celebrated.

claims.text: Galileo muttered "And yet it moves" as he got up from his knees.
claims.note: The line first appears in print in 1757, more than a century after the trial. No witness reports it.

claims.text: "What the barbarians didn't do, the Barberini did."
claims.note: The joke was going round Rome in his lifetime and is linked to Pasquino, the statue where Romans pinned anonymous jibes. Who coined it is unknown.

claims.text: Urban turned on Galileo because he felt mocked as Simplicio.
claims.note: Contemporaries said so, and the pope's argument does end up in Simplicio's mouth. Historians also point to politics: Urban was under attack for being soft on heresy.

reigns.hook: Urban's nephews have made a lot of enemies. The next conclave picks a stern old Roman lawyer who owes them nothing, and who listens rather too closely to his sister-in-law.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Urban VIII
reigns.previously: Urban VIII dies in 1644, and many Romans cheer.
paragraphs: Giovanni Battista Pamphili was a Roman lawyer and papal diplomat, plain-faced, slow and suspicious. France tried to block him, but the veto came too late. Once elected he went after Urban's nephews and their fortune, and they fled to France. Everyone said the real power was his widowed sister-in-law, Olimpia Maidalchini. Ambassadors learned to call on her first.

In 1648 the Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years War and gave Protestant states rights in law. Innocent declared it null and void. Europe ignored him. The days when a pope could undo a peace treaty were over.

His family palace stood on Piazza Navona, so he turned the square into a showpiece. Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers went up in the middle, finished in 1651. In 1650 Velázquez painted him, red-faced and wary, one of the great portraits of all time. He died in January 1655.

claims.text: Seeing his portrait, Innocent said "Troppo vero!", "Too true!"
claims.note: A much-repeated story with no contemporary source. He did hang the picture and reward the painter.

claims.text: Olimpia Maidalchini ran the Church through him and was nicknamed "the popess".
claims.note: Her influence was real and widely reported by envoys. The juiciest tales come from hostile gossip writers such as Gregorio Leti.

claims.text: Olimpia refused to pay for his coffin, saying she was a poor widow.
claims.note: Told by hostile writers after his death. His body did lie for days before burial, but the details are coloured.

reigns.hook: Innocent is barely buried when a remarkable guest sets out for Rome: a queen who has given up her throne to become a Catholic.
