reigns.title: Queens, Sieges and Colonnades
reigns.tagline: Colonnades, a queen in exile and a city saved
reigns.previously: Innocent X dies in 1655, and his family squabbles over the bill.
paragraphs: Alexander VII, Fabio Chigi, had sat through the Westphalia talks as papal envoy and seen the old order crack. He made his mark in stone: Bernini wrapped St Peter's Square in two great curving colonnades, like arms reaching out to the crowd. Rome also got a star convert. Queen Christina of Sweden, who had given up her crown, rode into the city in December 1655 and made it her home.

Clement IX, Giulio Rospigliosi, had written opera librettos in his younger days, including one of the first comic operas. Innocent XI was a sterner sort: thrifty, pious and locked in a long quarrel with Louis XIV. He poured money into the Holy League, and in 1683 the Polish king John III Sobieski smashed the Ottoman siege of Vienna.

Innocent XII went after the old family business. His bull of 1692 banned popes from handing estates, offices and income to their relatives, and allowed at most one relative to be made cardinal. He died in September 1700, with Rome grander than ever.

claims.text: Clement IX wrote opera librettos, including the comic opera Chi soffre speri.
claims.note: Rospigliosi wrote texts for operas staged by the Barberini in the 1630s and 1640s, decades before he became pope.

claims.text: Papal money helped save Vienna in 1683.
claims.note: Innocent XI sent large subsidies to the emperor and to Poland and worked hard to build the alliance. He was beatified in 1956.

claims.text: Innocent XII's bull of 1692 ended papal nepotism.
claims.note: The bull Romanum decet pontificem was real and largely obeyed. It did not end favouritism at court, but the age of the super-rich papal nephew was over.

reigns.hook: The new century opens with a new pope and an old fight. A movement of strict French Catholics, the Jansenists, is about to feel the papal hammer.

reigns.title: Popes in the Age of Reason
reigns.tagline: Fountains, philosophers and the fall of the Jesuits
reigns.previously: Innocent XII dies in 1700, having banned papal nepotism on paper.
paragraphs: Clement XI fought on two fronts. In 1713 his bull Unigenitus condemned 101 statements from a book by the French Jansenist Pasquier Quesnel, splitting the French Church for decades. He also banned missionaries in China from letting converts honour Confucius and their ancestors with the old rites. The Chinese emperor was not impressed, and the missions withered.

Clement XII, who went blind soon after his election, started the Trevi Fountain in 1732 and in 1738 issued the first papal condemnation of Freemasonry. Benedict XIV, Prospero Lambertini, was the star of the century: a witty scholar admired even by enemies of the Church. Voltaire dedicated a play to him, and the pope wrote back to thank him.

Then the Catholic kings turned on the Jesuits, the pope's most loyal order. Portugal, France and Spain threw them out. In 1773 Clement XIV, a Franciscan, dissolved the whole Society of Jesus. He died the next year, and Rome whispered poison.

claims.text: Voltaire dedicated his play Mahomet to Benedict XIV, who thanked him.
claims.note: The dedication and the pope's polite reply of 1745 were printed. Voltaire was delighted to have a pope's letter to wave at his critics.

claims.text: Clement XIV was poisoned in revenge for suppressing the Jesuits.
claims.note: Rumours flew at once and his body decayed fast. The doctors found no proof, and most historians think he died of illness.

claims.text: The Trevi Fountain took 30 years to finish.
claims.note: Begun under Clement XII in 1732, it was finished in 1762 under Clement XIII.

reigns.hook: The Jesuits are gone and the conclave drags on for months. The man who comes out is handsome, vain and about to run straight into the French Revolution.

reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Clement XIV
reigns.previously: Clement XIV dies in 1774, amid whispers of poison.
paragraphs: Giovanni Angelo Braschi was handsome and knew it. He spent freely: a new sacristy for St Peter's, galleries for the Vatican's ancient statues, a palace for his nephew and a costly scheme to drain the Pontine Marshes. In 1782 he travelled all the way to Vienna to talk Emperor Joseph II out of his Church reforms. Joseph was charming and changed nothing.

Then France exploded. In 1791 Pius condemned the Revolution's Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which turned priests into elected state officials. In 1796 a young general called Napoleon Bonaparte marched into Italy. The Treaty of Tolentino in 1797 cost the pope land, millions in cash and a hundred works of art.

In February 1798 the French took Rome and declared a republic. Pius, 80 years old and sick, was hauled away as a prisoner, from town to town and over the Alps to Valence in France. He died there in August 1799.

claims.text: Many said Pius VI would be the last pope.
claims.note: The papacy looked finished in 1799, with Rome occupied and the pope dead in exile. Some French officials and writers said as much.

claims.text: He was vain about his good looks, especially his legs.
claims.note: A favourite joke of Roman satirists. His love of show and building is well documented; the vanity stories are gossip.

claims.text: The art taken at Tolentino went to the Louvre.
claims.note: Many pieces were paraded through Paris in 1798. After Napoleon fell, the sculptor Canova recovered much of it for Rome.

reigns.hook: The pope has died a prisoner and Rome is in French hands. The cardinals scatter, then gather in Venice under Austrian protection to elect a successor.

reigns.tagline: The monk who stood up to Napoleon

reigns.cameToPower: Elected at a conclave in Venice
reigns.previously: Pius VI dies a French prisoner at Valence in 1799.
paragraphs: Barnaba Chiaramonti was a Benedictine monk, gentle and stubborn, from Cesena like his predecessor. Back in battered Rome, he had to deal with Napoleon. Their Concordat of 1801 brought the Church back to France, on Napoleon's terms. In 1804 Pius crossed the Alps for the coronation in Notre-Dame. At the big moment, Napoleon took the crown and put it on his own head.

The friendship soured. In 1809 Napoleon annexed Rome. Pius excommunicated the invaders, and in the early hours of 6 July French troops broke into the Quirinal Palace and arrested him. He was held at Savona, then at Fontainebleau, and bullied into concessions he later took back.

When Napoleon fell, Pius came home to cheering crowds in May 1814. That August he restored the Jesuits, and the Congress of Vienna gave back most of the Papal States. He even gave Napoleon's mother a home in Rome. He died in August 1823, weeks after a fall that broke his hip.

claims.text: Napoleon crowned himself in front of the pope.
claims.note: Planned in advance and recorded by witnesses. Pius blessed the crown; David's huge painting shows Napoleon crowning Josephine instead.

claims.text: Pius called Napoleon "Commediante! Tragediante!" to his face.
claims.note: The scene comes from the French writer Alfred de Vigny, writing in 1835. No witness reported it.

claims.text: Pius sheltered Napoleon's mother and family in Rome.
claims.note: Letizia Bonaparte lived in Rome from 1814 until her death in 1836.

reigns.hook: Napoleon is gone, the Papal States are back, and the old guard means to keep them. The next popes will fight the modern world with police, censors and Austrian troops.

reigns.title: The Old Order Strikes Back
reigns.tagline: Police, censors and no railways
reigns.previously: Pius VII dies in 1823, his lands restored.
paragraphs: Leo XII, Annibale della Genga, ran the restored Papal States like a strict headmaster. Rome's Jews were shut back into the ghetto, wine shops were restricted and police spies hunted secret societies like the Carbonari. His successor, Pius VIII, lasted less than two years.

Gregory XVI, a monk elected in February 1831, faced revolution within days. Bologna and other towns rose up and declared the pope's rule over. He called in Austrian troops to crush them. In 1832 his encyclical Mirari vos condemned liberalism, freedom of the press and freedom of conscience.

He kept the Papal States one of the most old-fashioned corners of Europe, with priests in charge of almost everything. He would not even let railways in. When he died in June 1846, Italy was simmering with nationalism, and the cardinals wanted a gentler face.

claims.text: Leo XII banned vaccination against smallpox.
claims.note: Often repeated, but historians have found no clear ban; the story may come from his opponents' propaganda.

claims.text: Gregory XVI called railways "chemins d'enfer", roads to hell, a pun on the French chemins de fer.
claims.note: A good joke and widely told, but no reliable source has him saying it.

claims.text: Gregory XVI kept railways out of the Papal States.
claims.note: The first line in papal territory opened only in 1856, under his successor.

reigns.hook: The cardinals pick a kindly bishop with a name for liberal ideas. Italy goes wild for him. It won't last.

reigns.tagline: From liberal hero to prisoner of the Vatican
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Gregory XVI
reigns.previously: Gregory XVI dies in 1846, with railways still banned.
paragraphs: Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, soon "Pio Nono", began as Italy's liberal hero. He freed political prisoners and eased censorship. Then came 1848. His minister Pellegrino Rossi was stabbed to death on the steps of parliament, and Pius slipped out of Rome in disguise to Gaeta. Mazzini and Garibaldi set up a Roman Republic until French troops crushed it in 1849. Pius came home cured of liberalism.

He dug in. In 1854 he declared the Immaculate Conception a dogma. In 1858 papal police took six-year-old Edgardo Mortara from his Jewish family in Bologna, because a servant said she had secretly baptised him. Pius refused every plea to return him. In 1864 his Syllabus of Errors denied that the pope should make peace with progress and liberalism.

In July 1870 the First Vatican Council declared the pope infallible when defining doctrine. On 20 September Italian troops blasted through the wall at Porta Pia and took Rome. The Papal States were gone after 1,100 years. Pius shut himself in the Vatican and called himself a prisoner. He reigned 31 years, the longest after Peter's traditional span.

claims.text: Edgardo Mortara was taken from his parents and raised by the Church.
claims.note: The case caused an international outcry. Mortara became a priest and defended the pope all his life.

claims.text: Infallibility passed by 533 votes to 2.
claims.note: Many opposing bishops left Rome before the final vote on 18 July 1870 rather than vote against the pope.

claims.text: In 1881 a mob tried to throw his coffin into the Tiber.
claims.note: During the night-time move of his body to San Lorenzo, anticlerical rioters attacked the procession. Police drove them off.

reigns.hook: Pio Nono dies after 31 years. The cardinals want a short, quiet reign and pick a frail-looking man of 67. He will outlive almost all of them.

reigns.tagline: The stopgap pope who lasted 25 years
reigns.previously: Pius IX dies in 1878, the self-styled prisoner of the Vatican.
paragraphs: Vincenzo Gioacchino Pecci was 67, thin and pale, and the cardinals expected a short reign. He lasted 25 years. He stayed a prisoner of the Vatican and never set foot in Italian Rome, but his mind roamed further. In 1881 he opened the Vatican's secret archives to scholars of every faith.

In 1891 his encyclical Rerum Novarum took on the industrial age. It defended private property against socialism, but it also said workers deserved a fair wage and had the right to form unions. It became the founding text of modern Catholic social teaching.

He was the first pope to be filmed, blessing the camera in the Vatican gardens in 1896. He also enjoyed Vin Mariani, a French tonic wine laced with coca, and let his face appear in its adverts. He died in July 1903, aged 93.

claims.text: Leo XIII endorsed a cocaine-laced wine.
claims.note: Vin Mariani's adverts used his picture and said he had awarded its maker a gold medal. Coca wine was legal and fashionable at the time.

claims.text: He was the first pope filmed and recorded.
claims.note: Film of him from the 1890s survives, as does a wax-cylinder recording of his voice made in 1903.

reigns.title: A Saint and a Peacemaker
reigns.tagline: A vetoed favourite, a saint and a war nobody would stop
reigns.previously: Leo XIII dies in July 1903, aged 93.
paragraphs: Rampolla was leading the votes when Cardinal Puzyna of Kraków read out a veto from Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria. The cardinals protested, then elected Giuseppe Sarto, patriarch of Venice and son of a village postman. As Pius X, one of his first acts was to ban such vetoes, on pain of excommunication.

Pius X was warm with ordinary people and fierce with theologians. He branded new critical approaches to the Bible and doctrine "modernism", the sum of all heresies, and in 1910 made every priest swear an oath against it. He let children take communion young. He died in August 1914 as the war began, and in 1954 he was declared a saint.

Benedict XV, Giacomo della Chiesa, spent his reign trying to stop the war. In August 1917 he sent a peace note to all sides, calling it a useless slaughter. Nobody listened, and each side suspected him of favouring the other. He also issued the first Code of Canon Law in 1917, and died of pneumonia in January 1922.

claims.text: Austria vetoed the favourite, Rampolla, in 1903.
claims.note: The last use of the old Catholic powers' veto. Rampolla's votes actually rose after it was read, but he could not win.

claims.text: Benedict XV called the war a "useless slaughter".
claims.note: The words are in his peace note of 1 August 1917, addressed to the leaders of the warring nations.

claims.text: The Allies secretly agreed to keep the pope out of the peace talks.
claims.note: Article 15 of the secret Treaty of London of 1915, made public by the Bolsheviks in 1917, shut out the Holy See at Italy's request.

reigns.hook: Benedict is dead. The cardinals turn to a librarian who climbs mountains. Down in Rome, a former socialist journalist named Mussolini is months from power.

reigns.tagline: The mountaineer pope who made a country
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Elected; made cardinal by Benedict XV
reigns.cameToPower: Elected on the fifth day of conclave
reigns.previously: Benedict XV dies of pneumonia in January 1922.
paragraphs: Achille Ratti was a scholar-priest who ran the Ambrosian Library in Milan and then the Vatican Library, and spent his holidays climbing Monte Rosa, the Matterhorn and Mont Blanc. After a stint as papal envoy in newly independent Poland, he became archbishop of Milan and, in February 1922, pope. That October, Mussolini came to power.

On 11 February 1929 his Secretary of State and Mussolini signed the Lateran Treaty. Italy recognised a tiny sovereign state, Vatican City, and paid compensation for the lost Papal States. The pope accepted the loss of Rome. The Roman Question was settled. In 1931 Marconi himself helped open Vatican Radio.

In 1933 he signed a concordat with Hitler's Germany, negotiated by Eugenio Pacelli. The Nazis broke it almost at once. In 1937 his encyclical Mit brennender Sorge, written in German, was smuggled into the country and read from Catholic pulpits on Palm Sunday. Old and ill, he was preparing an encyclical against racism and antisemitism when he died in February 1939.

claims.text: He died before he could publish an encyclical against racism and antisemitism.
claims.note: A draft, later called the "hidden encyclical", was written by Jesuits at his request in 1938. It was never issued.

claims.text: Mit brennender Sorge was smuggled into Germany and read out on Palm Sunday 1937.
claims.note: Copies were secretly printed and carried to parishes. The Gestapo seized what it could afterwards.

claims.text: He told Belgian pilgrims in 1938: "Spiritually, we are Semites."
claims.note: Reported by Belgian Catholic papers at the time; the Vatican's own paper left it out.

reigns.hook: Pius XI is dead and Europe is months from war. The cardinals choose the man who knows Germany best: his Secretary of State, Eugenio Pacelli.

reigns.tagline: The diplomat pope of the Second World War
reigns.previously: Pius XI dies with his encyclical against racism still unpublished.
paragraphs: Eugenio Pacelli was a Roman lawyer's son who spent his life in Vatican diplomacy. He was nuncio in Germany through the 1920s, then Pius XI's Secretary of State, and in 1933 he negotiated the concordat with Hitler's new government. The cardinals chose him on the third ballot, on his birthday, in March 1939. Six months later Germany invaded Poland.

He kept the Vatican formally neutral. In his Christmas message of 1942 he spoke of hundreds of thousands condemned to death or slow extinction, some only because of their nationality or race. He named neither the Jews nor Germany. On 16 October 1943 German troops rounded up Rome's Jews; more than a thousand were sent to Auschwitz. Thousands of others hid in Rome's convents, monasteries and Vatican properties.

After the war he was a fierce Cold War opponent of communism. In 1950 he declared the Assumption of Mary a dogma, the only time a pope has formally used papal infallibility since 1870. He died in October 1958. The argument over his wartime silence began a few years later and has never stopped.

claims.text: Pius XII did all he could for the Jews of Europe and directed the rescue in Rome.
claims.note: Critics such as John Cornwell (Hitler's Pope, 1999) say his silence failed the victims. Defenders, like the Jesuit Pierre Blet, point to the sheltering in Rome. Since the archives opened on 2 March 2020, David Kertzer (The Pope at War, 2022) and others have added evidence, and the debate goes on.

claims.text: His 1942 Christmas message spoke of people killed because of their nationality or race without naming Jews or Germany.
claims.note: The text of the broadcast survives. Some at the time read it as a clear protest; others found it too vague to matter.

claims.text: St Peter's bones were found under the basilica.
claims.note: Pius XII ordered the excavations and said in 1950 that Peter's tomb had been found; Paul VI said in 1968 the bones were identified. Many archaeologists remain unconvinced.

reigns.hook: The cardinals meet in October 1958. After nineteen years, many want a short, quiet pontificate. They choose a 76-year-old peasant's son from Venice.

reigns.tagline: The stopgap pope who threw open the windows
reigns.previously: Pius XII dies after nineteen years, the war still hanging over him.
paragraphs: Angelo Roncalli grew up in a big family of tenant farmers near Bergamo. He spent decades as a Vatican diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and France before becoming patriarch of Venice. At 76 he looked like a safe, short-term choice. He was round, funny and warm, and he took the name John, which an antipope of the Great Schism had used. He calmly declared himself the twenty-third.

Within three months he announced an ecumenical council. The Second Vatican Council opened on 11 October 1962. That night a huge crowd with candles filled St Peter's Square, and he spoke from his window about the moon, then told the parents to go home and give their children a hug from the pope. In April 1963 he issued Pacem in Terris, a letter on peace addressed to everyone of good will.
He was already dying of stomach cancer. He died on 3 June 1963, with the council barely begun. He was canonised in 2014.

claims.text: As a diplomat in Istanbul during the war he helped Jewish refugees escape.
claims.note: His help with transit papers and his contacts with Jewish agencies are well documented, though how many lives it saved is uncertain.

claims.text: He chose the number XXIII on purpose to settle that the Pisan John XXIII was not a real pope.
claims.note: He did say at his coronation that the name had been used by popes of doubtful legitimacy. Whether he meant it as a ruling on the Schism is argued over.

claims.text: He said he got the idea for the council in a sudden flash of inspiration.
claims.note: That is how he told it. Historians note the idea of a council had been floated in the Curia under Pius XI and Pius XII.

reigns.hook: The council has hardly started and its pope is dead. Who will finish it? The favourite is the archbishop of Milan, a careful, anxious man.

reigns.tagline: The first pope to fly, who gave away his crown
reigns.previously: John XXIII dies of cancer with Vatican II barely begun.
paragraphs: Giovanni Battista Montini was a Curia insider who had become archbishop of Milan. He steered Vatican II to its close in 1965. The Mass moved from Latin into local languages, and the Church opened up to other Christians, Jews and the modern world. He gave away the papal tiara for the poor; American Catholics bought it and it sits in Washington.

He was the first pope to fly. In 1964 he went to the Holy Land and embraced Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople. In 1965 the two lifted the excommunications of 1054. That year he told the United Nations: no more war, war never again. In 1970 a man with a knife lunged at him at Manila airport.

In 1968 Humanae Vitae upheld the ban on artificial contraception, and many Catholics simply ignored it. In 1978 he begged the Red Brigades to free his old friend Aldo Moro, but they killed him. Paul VI died three months later. He was canonised in 2018.

claims.text: He gave his tiara away and it ended up in Washington.
claims.note: He laid it on the altar of St Peter's in 1964. It was bought by American Catholics and is displayed at the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington.

claims.text: He was wounded in the Manila knife attack of 1970.
claims.note: The attack is certain. Officials played down any injury at the time; later accounts by his secretary said he was cut but hid it.

claims.text: He wrote to the Red Brigades "on my knees" to beg for Aldo Moro's life.
claims.note: His public letter of April 1978 survives and was printed in newspapers at the time.

reigns.hook: Paul VI is dead. The cardinals pick someone utterly different: a smiling patriarch of Venice who will last just over a month.

reigns.tagline: The smiling pope who lasted 33 days
reigns.previously: Paul VI dies at Castel Gandolfo after fifteen years.
paragraphs: Albino Luciani came from a poor family in the Dolomites and was patriarch of Venice. He was elected on the first day of the conclave and became the first pope with a double name, John Paul, honouring the two popes before him. He refused to be crowned and had a simple inauguration Mass instead. People loved his grin and his easy way of talking. They called him the smiling pope.

On the morning of 29 September 1978 he was found dead in bed. He had died during the night, after 33 days as pope. The Vatican said a heart attack and there was no autopsy. Its first statements were muddled about who found him and what he was reading, and the confusion fed rumours for decades. In 2022 Francis beatified him.

claims.text: John Paul I was murdered to stop him cleaning up the Vatican Bank.
claims.note: Popularised by David Yallop's book In God's Name (1984). John Cornwell's investigation, A Thief in the Night (1989), and later Vatican research concluded he died naturally, but with no autopsy doubts survive.

claims.text: The Vatican first said his secretary found him, when in fact it was a nun.
claims.note: The Vatican later admitted that Sister Vincenza Taffarel, who brought his morning coffee, found the body.

reigns.hook: Two popes dead in two months. The shaken cardinals meet again, and this time they look beyond Italy for the first time in 455 years.

reigns.tagline: The Polish pope who outlasted communism
reigns.previously: John Paul I is found dead after 33 days. A second conclave meets.
paragraphs: Karol Wojtyła had been an actor, a quarry worker under Nazi occupation and then archbishop of Kraków. He was the first non-Italian pope since Adrian VI. In June 1979 he went home to communist Poland and millions came to hear him. A year later the Solidarity movement was born. When the regimes of Eastern Europe fell in 1989, many gave him part of the credit.

On 13 May 1981 Mehmet Ali Ağca shot him in St Peter's Square. He nearly died. In 1983 he visited Ağca in prison and forgave him. He made over 100 foreign trips, started World Youth Days. He was strict on doctrine and made a record number of saints.

Late in his reign the abuse crisis began to break, with the 2002 revelations in Boston. His final years were a public decline with Parkinson's disease. At his funeral crowds chanted "Santo subito", sainthood now. He was canonised in 2014.

claims.text: The Soviet bloc was behind the 1981 assassination attempt.
claims.note: Ağca's stories changed constantly. An Italian court acquitted three Bulgarians in 1986, and no firm proof of a Soviet order has emerged.

claims.text: He believed the Virgin of Fátima saved his life.
claims.note: He said so himself: the shooting fell on the anniversary of the first Fátima apparition. A bullet was later set in the crown of the Fátima statue.

claims.text: He was slow to act against abusers, notably Marcial Maciel.
claims.note: Maciel, founder of the Legion of Christ, was only ordered to retire to a life of prayer in 2006, under Benedict XVI. A 2020 Vatican report found John Paul II was misled over Theodore McCarrick; critics say he ignored warnings.

reigns.hook: John Paul II is dead after nearly 27 years. The man who ran his doctrine office, a shy German professor, says the funeral Mass.

reigns.tagline: The professor who did the unthinkable and resigned
reigns.previously: John Paul II dies after nearly 27 years. Crowds cry "Santo subito".
paragraphs: Joseph Ratzinger was a Bavarian policeman's son. As a teenager he was enrolled in the Hitler Youth, compulsory by then, and was drafted into an anti-aircraft unit. He became a leading theologian and, for 24 years, John Paul II's guardian of doctrine. In 2006 he gave a lecture in Regensburg quoting a Byzantine emperor's attack on Islam, and protests broke out across the Muslim world.

The abuse crisis dominated his years: in Ireland, Germany, the United States. He met survivors, wrote to Ireland's Catholics in 2010 and removed hundreds of abusive priests. In 2012 he sent the first papal tweet.

On 11 February 2013 he told a meeting of cardinals, in Latin, that he was resigning. No pope had stepped down since Gregory XII in 1415, and none of his own free will for centuries. That evening lightning struck the dome of St Peter's. He lived on as pope emeritus until his death on 31 December 2022.

claims.text: Lightning hit St Peter's dome on the night he announced his resignation.
claims.note: It was photographed by news agency photographers. Many took it as a sign; it was a storm.

claims.text: As archbishop of Munich he mishandled abuse cases.
claims.note: A 2022 report for the archdiocese said he failed to act in four cases. He apologised to victims but denied any cover-up.

claims.text: He was a Nazi.
claims.note: Hitler Youth membership was compulsory for boys his age. Biographers find no sign he supported the regime; his family was opposed to it.

reigns.hook: The chair is empty, and its last occupant is still alive. The cardinals look to the other end of the world.

reigns.tagline: The pope from the end of the world
reigns.previously: Benedict XVI resigns, the first pope to do so in nearly 600 years.
paragraphs: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, archbishop of Buenos Aires, was the first Jesuit pope, the first from the Americas and the first from outside Europe since the 8th century. He was the first to take the name Francis. He skipped the papal apartments and lived in the Santa Marta guesthouse. Asked in 2013 about gay priests, he answered: who am I to judge?

His 2015 encyclical Laudato si' made climate change a moral issue. In March 2020, with Italy locked down by COVID, he prayed alone in a rain-soaked, empty St Peter's Square. He made mistakes on abuse, notably defending a Chilean bishop in 2018, then apologised and changed course, making Church officials report abuse.
In early 2025 he spent five weeks in hospital with pneumonia. On Easter Sunday, 20 April, he gave the blessing from the balcony and rode through the crowd. He died the next morning, aged 88.

claims.text: He was runner-up to Ratzinger in the 2005 conclave.
claims.note: Based on an anonymous cardinal's diary leaked to an Italian journalist. Conclave votes are secret.

claims.text: He gave his Easter blessing and died the next morning.
claims.note: The Vatican announced his death on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, from a stroke and heart failure.

reigns.hook: Francis is dead. 133 cardinals gather in the Sistine Chapel, and the world wonders whether the next pope will carry on his work.

reigns.tagline: The first pope from the United States
reigns.previously: Francis dies on Easter Monday, the day after his last blessing.
paragraphs: Robert Francis Prevost was born in Chicago in 1955. He joined the Augustinian friars, was ordained a priest and spent many years as a missionary in Peru, where he later became bishop of Chiclayo and took Peruvian citizenship. He also served two terms as head of the Augustinian order worldwide. Francis brought him to Rome to run the Dicastery for Bishops, the office that vets new bishops.

The conclave met on 7 and 8 May 2025 and elected him on the fourth ballot. He was the first pope from the United States. He took the name Leo, and two days later told the cardinals why: Leo XIII had answered the industrial revolution, and the Church now had to face another revolution, artificial intelligence.

claims.text: He was elected on the fourth ballot, on the second day of the conclave.
claims.note: White smoke on 8 May 2025; the Vatican announced the result from the loggia of St Peter's that evening.

claims.text: He chose the name partly in honour of Leo XIII, because of artificial intelligence.
claims.note: He said so himself in his address to the College of Cardinals on 10 May 2025.

claims.text: He holds Peruvian as well as American citizenship.
claims.note: He became a Peruvian citizen in 2015, while serving in Chiclayo.
